hook: This entry is filed under a person's name rather than a number, and its very first line assures you that Dr. Michaels is not in danger. It comes from the Department of Miscommunications, which handles information that can't be said outright, so the document is written to imply its rules rather than state them. Read it like a puzzle and trust nothing at face value, starting with the warm-up exercise at the top.
whyItMatters:
The piece is a good showcase for a format where the real story lives in what is withheld. The tags place it in a miscommunications series and mark it as esoteric-class, and its whole method is to let contradictions and footnotes carry the information the main text refuses to deliver.

It rewards a second read more than most files. On a first pass it looks like a routine wellness check on a staff member; once you notice the cracks, nearly every sentence starts to mean something else.
thingsToNotice:
The opening inoculation pairs each true statement with its opposite, training you to read the file inversely: the title says he is not in danger, the description says he is an only child, and then in the interview he talks at length about a brother. That brother was taken in as a child, clung to him, would not let him leave, turned up hundreds of miles away when he moved, and has done the same to others; Michaels himself once called him a parasite.

The footnotes quietly list his whole research team as dead within about two days of each other, his foggy feeling began seconds after the first loss, and the interviewer keeps glancing at the space above his head. A flooded sub-level, a lost task-force member and the same fogginess in the rescuers hint that whatever is attached to him is spreading, which is why a custodial team sanitizes every room he leaves. His closing note insists he is fine while begging someone to understand and find a way out before someone slips up.
